scenes.animation: Night in a village in Odisha. A huge elephant quietly munches a banana plant in a farm while Zippy, on a scarecrow's hat, whispers in panic. Behind them, a shrinking forest turns brown and a waterhole dries up.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Neo! An elephant is eating the farmer's bananas! Why isn't it in the forest?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Because its forest is shrinking. When vegetation is scarce and waterholes dry up, elephants wander into farms looking for food like bananas and sugarcane.

scenes.animation: A map of India highlights Odisha, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Assam and Chhattisgarh. Roads and buildings cut through green forest patches; then a green 'Elephant corridor' band links two forests, and a herd walks safely along it, away from villages.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Changes in rainfall and temperature affect vegetation. Cutting trees for roads and buildings makes it worse.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So wildlife ecologists have marked corridors. These connect forest habitats, so elephants can travel between forests without conflict with people.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So one change in the forest reached all the way to a farmer's bananas!

scenes.animation: A teacher leads a group of students with notebooks to a pond and a big banyan tree; a 'Caution: explore in groups with your teacher' badge appears. A table titled 'Pond' and 'Forest' fills in: 'Living beings: fish, grass, trees, birds' and 'Non-living things: water, soil'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A habitat is simply a place where an organism lives. It could even be the bark of a tree.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Activity time. Explore in groups with your teacher. Pick two habitats, like a pond, a forest, a farm, or a large banyan, mango or pilkhan tree.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: List the living beings and the non-living things you see in each, and record them in a table.

scenes.animation: The table's columns re-label themselves: 'Living beings' glows green as 'Biotic components', 'Non-living things' glows blue as 'Abiotic components'. Underwater, a cartoon fish nibbles tiny plants (tag 'biotic need: food') and breathes oxygen from water (tag 'abiotic need: oxygen'). Frogs, turtles, snails, ducks, algae, duckweed and lotus pop in around it. An 'EXAM TIP' card appears.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The living beings in a habitat are its biotic components. The non-living things are its abiotic components.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A pond provides food, oxygen, shelter and space to grow. Fish get food, a biotic need, from small plants and animals, and oxygen, an abiotic need, from water.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: when classifying, remember that air, water, sunlight, soil and temperature are abiotic. Plants, animals and microbes are biotic.

scenes.animation: A forest split into day and night halves. On the warm day side, a rodent scurries for seeds; on the cool night side, a snake glides out. Both share the same tree. A label reads 'Same habitat, different conditions'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: If everyone shares one habitat, don't they get in each other's way?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Organisms use resources differently. A forest may be warm by day and cool at night.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A snake active at night and a rodent active by day live in the same habitat but face different conditions. That's how they coexist in harmony.

scenes.animation: Recap board with three ticks: '1. Habitat = place where an organism lives', '2. Biotic = living; Abiotic = air, water, sunlight, temperature, soil', '3. Different habitats offer different living conditions'. The elephant waves from inside its corridor.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: a habitat is the place where an organism lives.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: living beings are biotic components, while air, water, sunlight, temperature and soil are abiotic components.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: different habitats offer different living conditions, and organisms share them in harmony.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: And elephants get their own highway. Nice.

name: Populations, Communities and Why Every Organism Matters

scenes.animation: Zippy stares into a pond and counts fish on his fingers, running out of fingers. A caption reads 'Same kind of fish, lots of them!'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Twelve, thirteen... they all look the same! Is this one big fish family?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Scientists have a name for that crowd. It's called a population.

scenes.animation: A school garden. Students in four to five groups use string to mark a 1 m by 1 m square. Inside it, plants get counted with number bubbles. A table fills in: 'Plant 1: 20', 'Plant 2: 05', 'Animal 1', 'Animal 2'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A group of fish of the same kind living together in a pond is a population of that fish.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Let's record one. Divide the class into four to five groups. Mark an area of 1 metre by 1 metre in the school garden.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Count the organisms of each kind in that area and record them. Then compile the data from all groups.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Our square has 20 of one plant and only 5 of another!

scenes.animation: The pond zooms out: separate bubbles of fish, frogs, lotus and snails merge into one big circle labelled 'Community = different populations sharing a habitat'. A cutaway shows a flower with labels 'sepals', 'petals', 'stamens (male)', 'carpels (female)', and a bee carrying yellow pollen between flowers.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So a population is a group of the same type of organisms in a habitat at a given time.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A community is made of different populations sharing the same habitat. Plants, animals and microorganisms together form it, and they depend on one another.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: For example, wind, water, insects, bats and birds carry pollen from stamens to carpels. This is pollination, and it is essential for fruits and seeds.

scenes.animation: Two ponds side by side: Pond A with fish and many flowers around it, Pond B without fish and few flowers. Arrows build step by step: fish eat dragonfly larvae; dragonflies drop in Pond A; bees and butterflies increase; flowers get pollinated and make more seeds. Red arrows are direct effects, green arrows indirect effects.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Now a real study. Researchers compared Pond A, with fish and many flowering plants, and Pond B, without fish and fewer flowering plants.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Fish eat dragonfly larvae, so Pond A had fewer dragonflies. Dragonflies usually eat flies, bees and butterflies.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: With fewer dragonflies, there were more bees, flies and butterflies. They pollinate nearby flowers, so plants near ponds with fish may produce more seeds.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Wait, the fish never even touched the flowers!

scenes.animation: A web diagram connecting fish, dragonflies, pollinators and plants, with abiotic icons for temperature, water and nutrients around the edge. A fishing net rises from the pond with a question mark: 'Overfishing?'. An 'EXAM TIP' card slides in.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exactly. This shows how biotic and abiotic components interact and affect each other. So could overfishing by humans change this balance? Think about it.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: don't mix up population and community. Population is one kind of organism. Community is many different populations together.

scenes.animation: Recap board with three ticks: '1. Population = same type of organism, one habitat, one time', '2. Community = different populations sharing a habitat', '3. Fish → fewer dragonflies → more pollinators → more seeds'. Zippy wears a dragonfly costume and gets chased by a fish.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: a population is a group of the same type of organisms in a habitat at a given time.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: a community is made of different populations sharing the same habitat.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: every organism matters. Fish in a pond can even increase seed production in nearby plants.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Bad costume choice. Very bad.

scenes.animation: A busy pond scene freezes like a paused video. Glowing lines connect a frog to an insect, sunlight to the water surface, and an earthworm to moist soil. Zippy tries to untangle the lines and gets wrapped up.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Help! Everything here is connected to everything else!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: That's the point. Let's sort those connections into three kinds.

scenes.animation: A three-column table builds up, one example sliding into place at a time. 'Criterion 1: biotic and abiotic': earthworms live in moist soil; a fish lays eggs in water. 'Criterion 2: two abiotic': bright sunlight raises day temperature; sunlight makes water evaporate fast. 'Criterion 3: among biotic': a frog eats insects; a water snake eats fish; frogs and fish compete for insect larvae.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Criterion one: interactions between biotic and abiotic components. Earthworms live in moist soil, and a fish lays eggs in water.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Criterion two: interactions between two abiotic components. The day temperature is high due to bright sunlight, and water evaporates fast due to sunlight.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Criterion three: interactions among biotic components. A frog eats insects, a water snake eats fish, and frogs and fish may compete for small insect larvae.

scenes.animation: Nested circles grow outward: 'Individual' (one deer), 'Population' (a herd), 'Community' (deer, trees, birds), 'Ecosystem' (plus soil, water, air, sunlight). Then a landscape shows a small river (aquatic) winding past mountains, forest, grassland and farmland (terrestrial), with the farm tagged 'human-made'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The biotic and abiotic components in a habitat interact with each other to form an ecosystem.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Ponds, rivers and lakes are aquatic ecosystems. Forests, farms and even a large banyan tree are terrestrial ecosystems. Farmland is a human-made ecosystem.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So an ecosystem can be as big as a forest or as small as one tree?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Yes. Ecosystems can be large or small, and they overlap and interact.

scenes.animation: Two-way arrows: sunlight, carbon dioxide and water flow into a leaf making food; soil feeds roots; air gives oxygen to animals. Then reverse arrows: the plant releases oxygen, roots grip soil against erosion, and leaves keep the soil moist and cool the air.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Living things depend on non-living ones. Plants need sunlight, carbon dioxide and water to make food, and soil gives them nutrients.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: And non-living things are shaped by living ones. Plants release oxygen, roots hold soil and prevent erosion, and plants keep soil moist and help cool the air.

scenes.animation: A forest picture with a table: Deer, Hare, Vulture, Bengal Fox, Shikra, Squirrel, Mouse, Mushroom, Tree. The tree gets a 'Producer / Autotroph: auto = self, troph = food' badge. The animals get 'Consumer / Heterotroph: hetero = other' badges, then sort into 'Herbivore: deer, hare', 'Carnivore: leopard', 'Omnivore: crows, foxes, mice'. An 'EXAM TIP' card appears.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Let's classify. Using the library or internet, find out what each forest organism eats, and fill in the table.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Plants make their own food by photosynthesis, so they are producers, or autotrophs. Organisms that depend on others for food are consumers, or heterotrophs.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Herbivores like deer and hare eat only plants. Carnivores like the leopard eat only animals. Omnivores like crows, foxes and mice eat both.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: learn the word meanings. Auto means self, hetero means other, and troph means food.

scenes.animation: Recap board with three ticks: '1. Three kinds of interactions: biotic-abiotic, abiotic-abiotic, biotic-biotic', '2. Ecosystem = biotic + abiotic interacting; aquatic or terrestrial', '3. Producers (autotrophs) and consumers (heterotrophs)'. Zippy finally untangles himself.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: interactions happen between biotic and abiotic parts, between two abiotic parts, and among biotic parts.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: biotic and abiotic components interacting together form an ecosystem, which can be aquatic or terrestrial.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: producers make their own food; consumers are herbivores, carnivores or omnivores.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Untangled. I'm an ecosystem expert now.

name: Food Chains, Food Webs and Decomposers

scenes.animation: A grassland lunch queue: grass waits nervously, a hare nibbles it, then a leopard eyes the hare. Zippy holds a clipboard titled 'Who eats whom?' and ducks behind a bush.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: I'm doing a survey. Question one: who's eating whom around here?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Good question. The answer draws a food chain.

scenes.animation: On a grassland card, pictures of grass, frog, hare, grasshopper, snake and eagle appear. Arrows draw themselves: 'Grass → Hare → Leopard' first, then a second chain builds link by link: 'Grass → Grasshopper → Frog → Snake → Eagle'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In a grassland, grass is eaten by the hare, and the hare is eaten by the leopard. That is a food chain.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Activity: take grass, frog, hare, grasshopper, snake and eagle, and draw arrows for who eats whom.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: One answer is grass to grasshopper to frog to snake to eagle. A food chain is a simple sequence showing who eats whom in an ecosystem.

scenes.animation: A crop field with many millet plants, fewer mice and one eagle. A counting table appears, then the numbers stack into a pyramid: millet at the wide base, mice in the middle, eagle at the narrow top. Side labels read 'Trophic level 1: producers', '2: herbivores', '3: small carnivores', 'next: large carnivores'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Now count the millet plants, mice and eagles in a crop field. Put the highest number at the base and the lowest at the top. What do you get?

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: A pyramid! Lots of millet, fewer mice, and one eagle on top.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Each position in a food chain is a trophic level. Producers are at the first level, herbivores like hares and deer at the second, small carnivores like frogs at the third, and large carnivores like tigers or vultures at the next.

scenes.animation: Grasses, mouse, hare, grasshopper, frog, bird, snake, owl, fox and hawk are scattered on a board. Several food chains are drawn in different colours, and they start sharing organisms; arrows multiply until the chains form a net labelled 'Food web'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In a real ecosystem, each organism may be eaten by two or more types of organisms.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So food chains are interlinked, forming a network called a food web.

scenes.animation: Rainy season: mushrooms pop up on a fallen log, and beetles and flies work on a pile of elephant dung. Zoom in: fungi and bacteria break big molecules into small pieces, which sink into the soil as glowing nutrient dots that roots then absorb. Tag: 'sapro = rotten, troph = food'. An 'EXAM TIP' card appears.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: What about dead matter and waste? Fungi like mushrooms and bacteria break down complex substances in dead plants and animals into simpler ones.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Beetles and flies on elephant dung help too. This is decomposition, and these organisms are decomposers, or saprotrophs.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Decomposers return nutrients to the soil. In nature, nothing is wasted.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: in food chain questions, arrows point from the organism eaten to the one that eats it.

scenes.animation: Recap board with three ticks: '1. Food chain = who eats whom; food web = interlinked chains', '2. Trophic levels: producers → herbivores → small carnivores → large carnivores', '3. Decomposers (saprotrophs) recycle nutrients'. Zippy's clipboard now shows a food web.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: a food chain shows who eats whom, and interlinked food chains form a food web.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: producers are at the first trophic level, then herbivores, then carnivores.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: decomposers, or saprotrophs, break down dead matter and recycle nutrients.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Survey complete. Nobody wanted to eat me.

name: Balance in Ecosystems: Chain Reactions and Relationships

scenes.animation: Zippy flicks one domino labelled 'Pond pollution'. It knocks down 'Plants die', 'Less oxygen', 'Fish die', 'More insects', 'Pests damage crops', 'More pesticides'. Zippy stares at the fallen line.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: I only touched one domino. How did the whole line fall?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: That's how ecosystems work. One small change leads to many others.

scenes.animation: A pond flowchart builds arrow by arrow: pollution kills plants, oxygen bubbles fade, fish float away, insects swarm out to nearby farmland, and a farmer sprays pesticide, which drips back into the soil and water.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Suppose many plants in a pond die because of pollution. Fewer plants make less oxygen in the water, so the fish population drops.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: With fewer fish, insects increase and spread to nearby farms. Farmers are then compelled to use pesticides, which may harm the environment again.

scenes.animation: A 1980s newspaper headline: 'India exports frog legs'. An Indian bullfrog, labelled 'Hoplobatrachus tigerinus', disappears from paddy fields; insect pests swarm the crops; pesticide cans multiply. A government stamp 'Export banned' thumps down.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: This really happened. In the 1980s, India was a big exporter of frog legs, especially of the Indian bullfrog.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Frog numbers fell. Since frogs eat insects, agricultural pests rose, and farmers used more synthetic pesticides, harming soil, water and health.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So the Government of India banned the export of frog legs.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Frogs were the farmers' free pest control all along!

scenes.animation: Deer and other animals jostle at one waterhole and plants stretch for sunlight, labelled 'Competition: food, water, space, sunlight'. A see-saw labelled 'Ecosystem balance' stays level. A text card reads 'Balance is dynamic, not fixed'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: An ecosystem is in balance when interactions keep populations and resources stable. This balance is dynamic, not fixed.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Organisms also compete for food, water, space or sunlight. Competition controls population size. Without it, one species could multiply too much.

scenes.animation: Three panels with plus and minus signs. 'Mutualism': a bee sips nectar (+) while the flower gets pollinated (+). 'Commensalism': an orchid gets support on a tree (+), the branch is unaffected (0). 'Parasitism': a tick feeds on a dog's blood (+), the dog gets skin irritation (−). An 'EXAM TIP' card slides in.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: There are other relationships too. In mutualism, both benefit, like honeybees and flowers.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In commensalism, one benefits and the other is not affected, like orchids on trees. In parasitism, one benefits and the other is harmed, like ticks on dogs.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: for these three, always write who benefits and who is harmed or unaffected, with one example each.

scenes.animation: Recap board with three ticks: '1. One change leads to another (frog legs → pests → pesticides)', '2. Competition keeps populations in check; balance is dynamic', '3. Mutualism (+,+), commensalism (+,0), parasitism (+,−)'. Zippy stands the dominoes back up.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: in an ecosystem, one change leads to another, like the frog legs story.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: competition controls population size and keeps the balance, which is dynamic.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: in mutualism both benefit, in commensalism one benefits and one is unaffected, and in parasitism one benefits while the other is harmed.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Dominoes restored. Nobody touch anything.

name: Benefits of Ecosystems and Sustainable Farming

scenes.animation: Zippy lists his morning on a scroll: fresh air, water, rice, a cotton shirt, a wooden desk, medicine. Each item flies back to a forest or a river. Zippy's scroll ends with 'Thank you, ecosystems?'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: My breakfast, my shirt and my desk all came from nature?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Yes. Ecosystems quietly support us every single day.

scenes.animation: Icons pop out of a forest: fresh air, fertile soil, food, fibres, timber, medicines. A lake gives water and fish. A family picnics by a river, labelled 'aesthetic and recreational value'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Forests provide fresh air, fertile soil, food, fibres, timber and medicines. Aquatic ecosystems provide water and food.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Ecosystems also have aesthetic and recreational value. But when we overuse or misuse resources, we disturb nature's balance.

scenes.animation: A map where the Ganges and Brahmaputra meet between India and Bangladesh, zooming into mangrove roots. Mangroves block storm waves and wind, absorb carbon dioxide and release oxygen. A 'UNESCO World Heritage Site, 1987' badge appears, then threats: axes, poachers, sewage pipes. A strip of protected areas follows: Jim Corbett, Manas, Chilika, Keibul Lamjao.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The Sundarbans have the largest mangrove forests in the world, where the Ganges and Brahmaputra meet. They slow down strong winds and waves during storms and floods.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: UNESCO declared them a World Heritage Site in 1987. But mangroves are cut for fuelwood and farming, and pollution and illegal hunting harm them.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Protected areas, like national parks, wildlife sanctuaries and biosphere reserves, help save such habitats.

scenes.animation: A timeline: '1950 to 1965: food crisis'. Tractors, fertiliser sacks and pesticide cans roll in under a 'Green Revolution' banner and grain piles rise. Then warning icons appear: overused chemicals, falling groundwater, and one crop repeated field after field, labelled 'Monoculture'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Humans also build ecosystems, like fish ponds, farms and parks. These need human care and management.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Between 1950 and 1965, India faced a food crisis. Tractors, synthetic fertilisers and pesticides raised food production. This was the Green Revolution.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: But overusing chemicals, pumping too much groundwater and growing only one crop are now seen as unsustainable.

scenes.animation: Students with a teacher interview a farmer under a neem tree, with question cards: 'How have your practices changed?', 'Effects of synthetic fertilisers and pesticides?', 'Changes in soil health?'. A cutaway of soil shows humus and friendly microbes fading, then a beetle eating pests. An ancient palm-leaf manuscript glows: 'Vrikshayurveda: Kunapa Jala'. An 'EXAM TIP' card appears.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Activity: visit a farm with your parents or teacher. Ask farmers how their practices changed, and what fertilisers and pesticides did to their soil. Then write a report.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Overusing synthetic fertilisers can reduce friendly microbes and humus, making soil prone to erosion. It can also reduce natural predators, so pests increase.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The ancient text Vrikshayurveda recommends nourishing soil with organic manure like Kunapa Jala. Today, some farmers are exploring organic and natural farming.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: growing the same crop repeatedly is called monoculture. It reduces biodiversity and affects pollinators.

scenes.animation: Recap board with three ticks: '1. Ecosystems give air, water, food, fibres, timber, medicines', '2. Sundarbans: largest mangroves, protect against storms, under threat', '3. Sustainable farming protects soil, predators and pollinators'. Zippy plants a sapling next to the farmer.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: ecosystems give us fresh air, water, food, fibres, timber and medicines.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: the Sundarbans, the largest mangrove forests in the world, protect us from storms but are under threat.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: sustainable farming protects soil health, natural predators and pollinators.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Thank you, ecosystems. No question mark this time.
